title: MHA, GQA, MQA and MLA
summary: Attention variants decide how many key and value heads a model stores. Fewer KV heads, or a compressed latent, shrink the KV cache and the memory traffic of decode, at some quality risk.
useIf: You compare open models for serving cost, or you must explain why two models of equal size need different GPU memory.
avoidIf: You call a hosted API and cannot see or change the attention design.

explain.md: In **multi-head attention (MHA)** every query head has its own key and value head. **Multi-query attention (MQA)** shares one KV head across all query heads, which greatly reduces the size of keys and values and the memory bandwidth of incremental decoding, at only minor quality loss [[tr10]]. **Grouped-query attention (GQA)** sits between them: more than one KV head but fewer than query heads. MHA checkpoints can be uptrained to GQA with about 5% of the original pre-training compute and reach quality close to MHA at a speed close to MQA [[r10]].

**Multi-head latent attention (MLA)**, used in DeepSeek-V2, takes a different route: it compresses keys and values into a latent vector. DeepSeek reports a 93.3% smaller KV cache and 5.76 times the maximum generation throughput compared with DeepSeek 67B, for a model with 236B total and 21B active parameters and a 128K context [[r11]]. That figure compares two different models, so it is not a like-for-like benchmark.

explain.title: Why fewer KV heads speed up decode
explain.md: Decode is memory-bandwidth-bound and re-reads the KV cache for every generated token. A smaller cache means fewer bytes to move per step and more sequences that fit in memory, so both TPOT and concurrency improve [[tr10]].

pitfalls.symptom: Two models of the same parameter count need very different GPU memory at 32K context
pitfalls.cause: Different KV head counts or layers change KV bytes per token
pitfalls.fix: Compute KV per token from each config before you size hardware [[r27]]

pitfalls.symptom: A migration to MQA lowers long-context answer quality
pitfalls.cause: Sharing a single KV head removes capacity that the task used
pitfalls.fix: Use GQA with a moderate group count, evaluate at your context lengths [[r10]]

pitfalls.symptom: An MLA model is slower than expected on your stack
pitfalls.cause: The engine runs a fallback attention path without MLA kernels
pitfalls.fix: Check the engine version and benchmark before committing

scenarios.title: Own MHA checkpoint, memory-bound serving
scenarios.situation: A team owns a trained MHA model and serves it on its own GPUs. KV memory caps concurrency. Retraining from scratch is out of the question, but a small training budget exists.
constraints: Quality must stay near the current level
unknowns: How much compute is 5% of pre-training for this model?
scenarios.question: What do you do?

options.name: Uptrain to MQA
options.why: It gives the largest KV cut.
options.tradeoff: More quality risk than GQA on tasks that use long-range detail.

options.name: Drop KV heads at inference with no retraining
options.why: The recovery of quality in the paper comes from uptraining, so skipping it is an untested risk.
options.tradeoff: Only acceptable as a throwaway experiment to see the memory effect.

options.name: Uptrain the checkpoint to GQA with a moderate group count
options.why: The published recipe reaches near-MHA quality at near-MQA speed for about 5% of the original compute.
options.tradeoff: It still costs training compute and needs an eval to confirm long-context quality.

flips.then: Quantize KV with an eval gate, or add GPUs.

flips.if: Quality drops on the long-context eval after uptraining
flips.then: Raise the number of KV groups.

scenarios.takeaway: GQA by uptraining is the cheap path from an MHA checkpoint.

scenarios.title: 128K context, GQA or MLA
scenarios.situation: A team must serve a 128K-token document workload at high concurrency. One candidate is a GQA model. The other uses MLA and advertises a very small cache.
constraints: Serving engine is fixed and supports both
unknowns: KV bytes per token measured on your engine
scenarios.question: How do you decide?

options.name: Choose the GQA model for mature support
options.why: It is the lower-risk path with predictable tooling.
options.tradeoff: You may leave memory and throughput on the table.

options.name: Choose MLA because it advertises the largest cache cut
options.why: A headline reduction against another model does not predict your quality or throughput.
options.tradeoff: Right once your own tests confirm the gain and the engine support.

options.name: Benchmark both at your context lengths for quality, KV bytes and throughput on your engine
options.why: The 93.3% figure compares DeepSeek-V2 with a different model, so only your own measurement answers the question.
options.tradeoff: It takes a day of testing.

flips.if: The engine has no efficient MLA path
Quality ties and MLA memory use is far lower in your test

scenarios.takeaway: Treat paper headlines as hypotheses. Measure on your own context lengths.

quiz.q: A model has 64 query heads and 8 KV heads. By what factor is its KV cache per token smaller than the same model with MHA?
quiz.explain: KV bytes scale with the number of KV heads. MHA would store 64, GQA stores 8, so the cache is 64 / 8 = 8 times smaller.

quiz.q: Match each attention variant to its defining idea.

pairs.r: Every query head has its own K and V
One KV head shared by all query heads
Groups of query heads share a KV head
KV compressed into a latent vector

quiz.explain: These are the standard definitions. GQA sits between MHA and MQA, and MLA compresses rather than shares.

quiz.q: A paper reports a 93.3% KV cache reduction for MLA. What is the correct way to use that number?
options: Assume any model with MLA has a cache 93.3% smaller than any GQA model
Apply it to a GQA model by changing the config
Treat it as a lead to test, since it compares DeepSeek-V2 with a different model
Ignore MLA because a 93.3% cut is impossible
quiz.explain: The figure is against DeepSeek 67B, a different design. It shows what is possible but does not predict your candidates. It cannot be applied to GQA by config, and the paper does report it, so it is not impossible.

flashcards.front: How does GQA differ from MHA and MQA?
flashcards.back: MHA gives every query head its own KV head, MQA shares one KV head across all, and GQA shares one KV head per group of query heads.

flashcards.front: What did the GQA paper show about converting MHA checkpoints?
flashcards.back: Uptraining with about 5% of pre-training compute reached quality near MHA at speed near MQA.
It compresses keys and values into a latent vector. DeepSeek-V2 reports a 93.3% smaller KV cache versus DeepSeek 67B.
